title: HostedAPI edge congestion + fanout interaction analysis
body:
Summary:
During 2028-03-16 16:03–17:12 UTC we observed a P0 degradation of the Hosted API characterized by sustained p95/p99 latency regressions and a burst of 5xx responses for streaming and short-text-generation routes. Impact lasted ~69 minutes with partial degradation continuing as increased error rates (~1.6% elevated) for the following 4 hours while mitigations rolled out.

Customer impact:
- External: Several customer applications reported increased TTFB and intermittent 5xx for streaming endpoints. Estimated customer-facing error budget burn: ~0.9%.
- Internal: Increased incident paging, surge in support tickets, automated canary rollbacks triggered in 2 orgs.
- Traffic affected: ~8% of total token throughput; concentrated on edge regions that handle multiplexed client connections.

How detected:
- Initial alert: automated p95 latency > 300ms alert from hosted-api-prod-observability at 16:04 UTC.
- Followups: streaming session disconnect rate spike visible in edge-proxy metrics; increased HTTP/2 RST_STREAM rates.

Immediate mitigation steps (timeline):
- 16:06 UTC: Oncall routed to SRE primary (Eleanor).
- 16:09 UTC: Disabled new allocation of tenant-level burst override policies (hotfix) to stop amplification of connection churn.
- 16:18 UTC: Scoped a temporary edge-proxy config rollback (previous stable) to reduce connection demultiplexing aggressive reuse optimization. 16:22 UTC: partial improvement in p95 observed.
- 16:30 UTC: Applied emergency increase to edge ephemeral socket backlog and lowered aggressive connection reuse threshold (tradeoff: slightly higher file descriptor usage).
- 16:46 UTC: Canaryed a fix in edge-proxy that prevents aggressive in-flight request fanout when tenant-level ratecap returns 429/503; this prevented retry storms.
- 17:05 UTC: Error rate returned to baseline in core regions, streaming reassembly failures subsided; continued monitoring.

Root cause (summary):
Primary cause: interaction between edge L7 connection multiplexing heuristics and tenant-level rate limiting produced amplifying fanout and connection churn. Specifically: when the ratecap subsystem rejected bursts (429s) under transient edge congestion, the proxy retried or attempted fanout to alternative backends in ways that caused many in-flight requests to remap, triggering TCP/TLS teardown churn and a cascade of RST_STREAM and 5xx responses.

Contributing factors:
- Edge connection reuse optimization (deployed 2028-02-28) prioritized multiplexing with a high concurrent-stream threshold. Under congestion this caused many logical streams to share faulty transport state leading to more session resets.
- Tenant-level burst policy misconfiguration: some tenants had permissive burst overrides that allowed client libraries to push short token-bursts which interacted poorly with the above multiplexing behavior.
- Observability blind spot: no direct metric correlated multiplexed-stream remap attempts to downstream ratecap responses; made root-cause correlation slower.
- Autoscaler cooldown interactions: the autoscaler reduced pod count mid-incident (autoscaler evaluation hit a stale metric window) which temporarily reduced available backend capacity and exacerbated 5xx.

Detailed timeline (key events, UTC):
- 16:03:48: first p95 alert triggered (hosted-api-observability).
- 16:05:12: edge-proxy RST_STREAM rate +420% vs baseline; streaming reassembly errors spike.
- 16:07:30: increased 429s returned from ratecap service for several tenants.
- 16:08:05: proxy began fanout to additional backend pods for in-flight requests; observed duplicate downstream attempts in traces.
- 16:12:20: autoscaler downscaled a backend service by 2 pods due to CPU-based policy (cooldown window misaligned).
- 16:18:00: rollback of edge multiplexing heuristic started.
- 16:46:00: candidate fix for retry/fanout suppression deployed to edge-proxy canary.
- 17:05:30: error metrics back to baseline; full mitigation confirmed at 17:12 UTC.

Why this wasn't prevented by our existing safeguards:
- Existing ratecap circuit-breakers assumed independent channel semantics and did not account for logical stream remapping inside the edge proxy.
- The rollout of the multiplexing heuristic lacked a targeted load-test that simulates tenant burst overrides combined with backend autoscaler churn.
- Alert thresholds were tied to aggregated p95 latency across regions rather than per-edge-proxy multiplexing failure signals.

Immediate action items (short-term mitigations already in progress):
- Disable multiplexing heuristic by default for affected regions until the fix is validated (owner: Aisha Patel, due: 2028-03-17).
- Push the edge-proxy change that suppresses fanout when upstream returns 429/503 and instead propagate backpressure to clients (owner: Miguel Ramirez, PR merged 2028-03-16).
- Adjust autoscaler cooldown window to favor min-stable-capacity during p95 spikes (owner: Samir Gupta, due: 2028-03-19).

Longer-term remediations and runbook updates (post-incident):
- Add a new metric and alert: multiplexed-stream-remap-rate and correlate with upstream ratecap responses; alert when remap_rate > 50/min and 429_rate > baseline (owner: Priya Nair, due: 2028-04-02).
- Update the rollout checklist to require combined scenarios: multiplexing + tenant-burst + autoscaler churn simulated in chaos testing (owner: eng-release, due: 2028-04-16).
- Harden tenant burst policy defaults: remove permissive overrides from self-serve signup and require review for large burst grants (owner: product-hosted-api, due: 2028-03-30).
- Add a dedicated diagnostic trace: request-level fanout lineage to quickly see duplicate downstream attempts in distributed traces (owner: observability, due: 2028-04-09).

Runbook changes (draft):
- New play: "edge-multiplex-fanout-degradation"
  - Detection: multiplexed-stream-remap-rate alert + streaming-reassembly-error rate spike
  - Immediate mitigations: disable multiplexing heuristic -> set edge-backlog to conservative -> suppress internal fanout on 429/503
  - Escalation path: SRE oncall -> edge-team -> ratecap service owner -> platform-autoscaler oncall

Postmortem notes and learnings:
- Complex interactions between optimization layers (proxy heuristics, rate limiting, autoscaling) can produce non-linear failure modes. We need more integrated integration tests and a higher-fidelity traffic simulator for multiplexed HTTP/2 behavior.
- Prefer to fail fast and surface backpressure to clients rather than attempt opaque internal retries and fanout when upstream signals congestion.
- Our rollout and telemetry practice should prioritize early signals for new proxy heuristics.

Follow-up ownership table (flat list of items):
- Aisha Patel: roll back multiplexing by default in affected regions; validate with canaries (due 2028-03-17).
- Miguel Ramirez: finalize and harden fanout suppression change in edge-proxy; run load-tests (done 2028-03-16, continue validation).
- Samir Gupta: update autoscaler cooldown policy and trigger retrospective runway test (due 2028-03-19).
- Priya Nair: add multiplexed-stream-remap metric + alert; update dashboards (due 2028-04-02).
- Product-hosted-api: tighten tenant burst override policy; ship change to signup/console (due 2028-03-30).
- Observability team: create a fanout lineage trace view and add to standard SRE triage dashboard (due 2028-04-09).

Appendix (evidence links and artifacts):
- Edge-proxy trace excerpts: linked in Confluence page (see linked_artifacts).
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/2178 (fanout suppression).
- JIRA: JIRA-SRE-4821 captures rollout checklist changes and test plan.

Notes for future incident drills:
- Run a scenario during chaos-week that combines tenant burst clients, induced backend autoscaler downscale, and edge multiplexing enabled.
- Add an SRE play exercise specifically on interpreting multiplexed-stream-remap_rate signals.

Conclusion:
This incident was driven by an optimization (edge multiplexing) that was not exercise tested across tenant burst patterns and autoscaler behaviors. The immediate mitigations and code changes reduce the risk of recurrence; longer-term fixes focus on improved telemetry, safer rollout practices, and policy hardening for tenant burst overrides.

Document history:
- Draft created 2028-03-16 by Eleanor Chen
- Collaborator updates 2028-03-17 (Aisha, Miguel)
- Finalized 2028-03-18
